Four, eight-ply nanocomposite panels were fabricated from Cycom 5575-2 glass with multi-walled carbon nanotube (MWNT) plies.
The control panel had eight plies of glass fabric reinforced composite only (8G).
The other three panels had differences in the placement of layers containing CNTs: 4G/4CNT, 2CNT/4G/2CNT, and (G/CNT)4.
The average EMI SE of type 2024 aluminum and type 7075 aluminum for the frequency range of 2 GHz – 18 GHz were 112.6 dB and 113.46 dB, respectively.
In a previous study, EMI SE values for four distinct nanocomposites containing nickel nanostrands (NS) were measured, with the averaged attenuation prior to testing ranging from 55 dB to 73 dB.
The EMI SE values for the MWNT nanocomposites prior to testing ranged from 0.33 dB for 8G to 87.5 dB for 4G/4CNT and 2CNT/4G/2CNT.
The final EMI SE values for the MWNT nanocomposites after testing ranged from 1.01 dB for 8G to 83.49 dB for 2CNT/4G/2CNT.
The thermal cycling consisted of 17,500 cycles between +60°C and -60°C, with each cycle having a total soak time of 20 seconds.

The failure mechanisms were consistent for each MWNT nanocomposite configuration, involving the initial formation of transverse fiber matrix cracks, delamination of CNT plies, and progression of transverse strand debonding.
The multi-walled CNTs remained intact even after the ultimate failure of the nanocomposite panels.
The vertical glass features observed in the 8G specimen may have contributed to its relatively low EMI shielding performance.
The EMI shielding measurements were taken in the frequency range of 2 GHz to 18 GHz before testing, and 8.2 GHz to 12.4 GHz during and after testing.
The 2CNT/4G/2CNT configuration provided the best EMI shielding performance among the MWNT nanocomposites, which is comparable to the nickel nanostrands configuration from a previous study.
The EMI SE properties for all four MWNT panels experienced varying degrees of reduction after thermal cycling and/or monotonic tension testing.
The cost of launching systems into space is extremely high, ranging from $10,000/lb to $12,000/lb, motivating the need for weight/cost reduction while maintaining performance.
